claims.claim_en: The verb فَاسْتَجَابَ placed at the opening of the phrase draws attention to the immediacy and effectiveness of God's response — a rhetorical shift of focus (iltifāt) that moves the discourse from the supplicants to the divine reaction.
claims.needs_review_reason: Verb‑first order is common in Arabic narrative; identifying it as iltifat depends on comparative context and on treating the verb as a deliberate rhetorical pivot rather than normal syntax.

claims.claim_en: The pairing of active and passive verbs (قَاتَلُوا … قُتِلُوا) creates a balanced antithesis/reciprocal parallel (muqābalah/tibāq) that highlights both the actors' struggle and their sacrifice; the mirrored forms reinforce the moral and eschatological reward promised.
claims.needs_review_reason: Labeling this pattern as muqabalah (balanced antithesis) is plausible, but the precise subtype (tibāq vs. muqābalah) may be debated among rhetoricians; the supporting source quote is a related verb form from the available commentary rather than the exact ayah phrasing.
